title: Biomass-derived biochar as a sustainable catalyst support for fuel desulfurization: a critical review of adsorptive and oxidative pathways toward ultra-low-sulfur fuels
content: Sulfur-containing compounds in transportation fuels remain a major environmental and industrial challenge because they generate SOx emissions, accelerate refinery corrosion, poison catalytic converters, and contribute to atmospheric pollution. Despite the fact that hydrodesulfurization (HDS) remains the dominant industrial desulfurization technology, its limited effectiveness toward sterically hindered sulfur compounds, particularly alkylated dibenzothiophenes such as 4,6-dimethyldibenzothiophene (4,6-DMDBT), has intensified the search for alternative deep-desulfurization technologies operating under mild conditions. Among these, adsorptive desulfurization (ADS) and oxidative desulfurization (ODS) have emerged as the most promising approaches, in which the physicochemical properties of the adsorbent or catalyst support largely determine the sulfur-removal efficiency. This review presents the first comprehensive and systematic comparison of biochar with conventional desulfurization materials, including γ-Al2O3, SiO2, and activated carbon, across both ADS and ODS systems. Beyond summarizing recent advances, this review establishes a unified mechanistic framework linking biochar's structure to its catalytic and adsorptive performance. Particular emphasis is placed on three interconnected structural characteristics that distinguish biochar from conventional supports: (i) abundant oxygen-containing functional groups that promote sulfur adsorption, anchor and disperse active metal species, and facilitate oxidant activation; (ii) a tunable hierarchical pore architecture and surface chemistry that enhance mass transport and accessibility of active sites; and (iii) strong metal–support interactions that improve metal dispersion, stabilize catalytically active phases, and promote the formation of highly active surface species during thermal treatment. Collectively, these characteristics enable biochar-supported systems to achieve highly efficient sulfur removal under mild operating conditions while offering a sustainable platform derived from renewable biomass. The review further establishes structure–property–performance relationships governing desulfurization efficiency and critically identifies the major barriers limiting industrial implementation, including catalyst deactivation, metal leaching, regeneration mechanisms, performance loss in real fuels, limited continuous-flow validation, and the scarcity of techno-economic and life-cycle assessments. Finally, future research priorities are proposed, including advanced surface engineering, multifunctional biochar composites, scalable catalyst design, and integrated green desulfurization processes. By providing a critical comparison with established support materials and a unified mechanistic perspective, this review demonstrates why biochar represents one of the most promising next-generation adsorbents and catalyst supports for sustainable fuel desulfurization.
